subChunks.title: Decomposition, Patterns & Algorithms
subChunks.hookHtml: Every spell in the Arcane Academy begins the same way — not with incantations, but with thought. Before you write a single line of code, you must learn to think like a machine.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is Computational Thinking?

Computational thinking is a problem-solving method built on four pillars:

  1. Decomposition — breaking a large problem into smaller, manageable pieces.
  2. Pattern Recognition — spotting similarities and repeated structures in problems.
  3. Abstraction — focusing only on the details that matter, ignoring the rest.
  4. Algorithmic Design — building a clear, step-by-step solution a computer can follow.

Decomposition

Imagine building a dungeon-crawler game. The problem looks enormous. Decomposition says: split it. Player movement. Enemy AI. Combat. Inventory. Level generation. Each becomes a smaller problem you can solve independently, then reassemble.

Pattern Recognition

Once you have small pieces, you notice that many share a structure. Both player and enemy need health, position, and an attack action. Recognising this pattern means you can write one solution and reuse it — the foundation of classes and interfaces in Java.

Abstraction

When you press W to move forward, you don't care how the screen pixel coordinates change — you just want the player to move. Abstraction hides the complexity. You interact with movePlayer(direction), not with raw pixel maths.

Algorithms and Pseudocode

An algorithm is a precise, finite sequence of steps that solves a problem. Before you write code, write pseudocode — a human-readable description of your algorithm:

ALGORITHM: find the highest score in a list
  SET maxScore = first item in list
  FOR each score in list:
    IF score > maxScore:
      SET maxScore = score
  RETURN maxScore

Pseudocode has no syntax rules — it just needs to be unambiguous. Writing pseudocode first forces you to think through edge cases (empty list? negative scores?) before the compiler catches errors for you.

Tracing Code

Tracing means simulating execution in your head (or on paper). Take each line, update a table of variable values, and note what gets printed or returned. This skill is essential for debugging and for answering 'what does this output?' questions. Practice it constantly.

storyBeats.text: The intake hall of the Arcane Academy is not lined with spellbooks. It is lined with puzzles — locks without obvious keys, mechanisms without obvious levers. A silver-haired wizard in deep blue robes watches you from the far end.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Veylan
storyBeats.text: Before you learn to speak to the machine, you must learn to think like one. Machines are utterly literal. They do exactly what you tell them — no more, no less. Most errors are not syntax mistakes. They are thinking mistakes.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Veylan
storyBeats.text: Computational thinking has four moves. First: decompose. When a problem overwhelms you, chop it apart. A dragon is terrifying whole, but you can cut it into head, neck, body, tail. Each piece becomes solvable.

storyBeats.speaker: Decomposing a spell-crafting system
storyBeats.text:
Spell system decomposed:
  → Ingredient selection
  → Ratio calculation
  → Element combination rules
  → Side-effect prediction
  → Power output measurement

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Veylan
storyBeats.text: Second: pattern recognition. Once you have pieces, you will notice they share shapes. A fireball and a lightning bolt both have a source, a direction, a damage value. One template. Two spells. A thousand spells, eventually. That is what classes will give you.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Veylan
storyBeats.text: Third: abstraction. When a guild member requests a portal, they do not want to know about ley-line mathematics. They want to say openPortal(destination) and step through. Hide the complexity. Expose only what matters.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Veylan
storyBeats.text: Fourth: algorithmic design. Write your solution as a precise series of steps before you touch the compiler. We call this pseudocode. It has no syntax — only clarity. The discipline of writing pseudocode first will save you more hours than any debugging tool.

storyBeats.speaker: Pseudocode: find the strongest rune in a collection
storyBeats.text:
ALGORITHM: findStrongestRune(runes)
  IF runes is empty: RETURN null
  SET strongest = runes[0]
  FOR each rune in runes:
    IF rune.power > strongest.power:
      SET strongest = rune
  RETURN strongest

Veylan steps aside, revealing a locked cabinet behind him. 'Every problem in this Academy,' he says, 'yields to these four moves. The machine does not guess. It follows instructions. Your job is to give it good ones.'

learningObjectives: Describe the four pillars of computational thinking: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic design
Break a real problem into smaller sub-problems using decomposition
Write unambiguous pseudocode for a simple algorithm
Trace a pseudocode algorithm step-by-step to determine its output
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to code without planning — leads to structural rework later
Confusing abstraction with oversimplification — abstraction hides complexity, it does not remove it
Writing pseudocode that is still ambiguous — 'process the data' is not a step; 'add each value to the total' is
Skipping the trace step and assuming logic is correct without verification
assessmentCriteria: Can name and briefly explain each of the four pillars of computational thinking
Can decompose a familiar problem (e.g. making tea) into at least five distinct steps
Can write pseudocode that is specific enough for another person to implement without asking questions
Can trace a given pseudocode algorithm on paper and determine the correct output
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain computational thinking to someone who has never written code. Use a non-programming example — like cooking a recipe or planning a journey — to illustrate decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic design.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The Academy's enchantment forge needs a restocking algorithm. When supplies run low, a golem must visit the market and purchase ingredients.

Your task: Write pseudocode for the following algorithm — restock the forge if any ingredient is below its minimum quantity. Your pseudocode must:

  • Check each ingredient in the forge's inventory
  • Compare its current quantity against a minimum threshold
  • If below threshold: calculate how much to buy (target quantity minus current), visit the market stall for that ingredient, and purchase the required amount
  • Output a summary line for each ingredient purchased
  • Output "Forge fully stocked" if nothing needed restocking

Write in plain English steps — no Java syntax required. Focus on precision and completeness.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
ALGORITHM: restockForge(inventory, minimums, targetQuantities)
  SET purchased = false
  FOR each ingredient in inventory:
    IF inventory[ingredient] < minimums[ingredient]:
      SET amountNeeded = targetQuantities[ingredient] - inventory[ingredient]
      GO TO market stall for ingredient
      PURCHASE amountNeeded units
      SET inventory[ingredient] = targetQuantities[ingredient]
      PRINT ingredient + ": purchased " + amountNeeded + " units"
      SET purchased = true
  IF purchased is false:
    PRINT "Forge fully stocked"
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
A different challenge: the Academy's spell matching system needs an algorithm.

Problem: Given a list of apprentices and a list of available spells (each spell has a minimum mana requirement), assign each apprentice to the most powerful spell they can cast without exceeding their mana capacity.

Your task: Write pseudocode for this matching algorithm from scratch. Consider: what happens if an apprentice cannot cast any spell? What if multiple spells fit within their mana capacity?

No hints this time. Think through the edge cases first, then write your pseudocode.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
ALGORITHM: assignSpells(apprentices, spells)
  SORT spells by manaRequirement DESCENDING  // try most powerful first
  FOR each apprentice in apprentices:
    SET assigned = false
    FOR each spell in spells:
      IF spell.manaRequirement <= apprentice.manaCapacity:
        ASSIGN spell to apprentice
        PRINT apprentice.name + " assigned: " + spell.name
        SET assigned = true
        BREAK  // stop at first (most powerful) matching spell
    IF assigned is false:
      PRINT apprentice.name + ": no spell available (insufficient mana)"

questions.questionHtml: Which pillar of computational thinking involves breaking a large problem into smaller parts?
questions.explanationHtml: Decomposition is the practice of splitting a complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems. This is often the first step in tackling any software challenge.

questions.questionHtml: What is the purpose of abstraction in computational thinking?
options: To find repeated structures across problems
To hide unnecessary complexity and expose only what matters
To write algorithms in plain English
questions.correctAnswer: To hide unnecessary complexity and expose only what matters
questions.explanationHtml: Abstraction lets you work at a higher level by hiding implementation details. You call movePlayer(direction) without caring how pixel coordinates are updated — that complexity is hidden behind a clear interface.

questions.questionHtml: Pseudocode must follow strict Java syntax rules to be valid.
questions.explanationHtml: Pseudocode is intentionally syntax-free. It only needs to be precise and unambiguous enough for a human (or future-you) to translate into real code. Its purpose is clarity of logic, not compilability.

questions.questionHtml: You are building a spell-crafting system. The system must handle ingredient selection, power calculation, side-effect prediction, and animation playback. Which computational thinking pillar does this planning step best illustrate?
questions.explanationHtml: Splitting the spell-crafting system into distinct responsibilities (ingredient selection, power calculation, etc.) is decomposition — taking one big problem and dividing it into independently solvable pieces.

questions.questionHtml: You notice that both Player and Enemy need health points, a position, and an attack method. Which pillar of computational thinking is helping you here?
questions.explanationHtml: Pattern recognition spots shared structure across different entities. Noticing that Player and Enemy share common attributes means you can build a shared base (an interface or superclass) and avoid repeating yourself.

questions.questionHtml: Trace this pseudocode: SET x = 3 / FOR i from 1 to 3: SET x = x * 2 / PRINT x. What is printed?
questions.explanationHtml: Tracing step by step: x starts at 3. Loop i=1: x = 3*2 = 6. Loop i=2: x = 6*2 = 12. Loop i=3: x = 12*2 = 24. PRINT 24.

questions.questionHtml: A fellow apprentice writes the pseudocode step: "Handle the user input." What is wrong with this step?
options: It uses natural language instead of Java syntax
It is too vague — a computer (or developer) cannot follow it without guessing
It should come at the end of the algorithm, not the middle
Nothing is wrong — pseudocode should be high level
questions.correctAnswer: It is too vague — a computer (or developer) cannot follow it without guessing
questions.explanationHtml: Good pseudocode must be unambiguous. "Handle the user input" does not say what to read, how to validate it, or what to do with the result. A better step would be: "READ username from input / IF username is empty: PRINT error and stop."

questions.questionHtml: When should you write pseudocode before writing Java code?
options: Only for algorithms longer than 100 lines
Only when working in a team
Whenever the logic is non-trivial — planning prevents structural rework later
Never — writing pseudocode wastes time that should be spent coding
questions.correctAnswer: Whenever the logic is non-trivial — planning prevents structural rework later
questions.explanationHtml: Writing pseudocode first is a discipline that pays off on any non-trivial problem. It forces you to think through edge cases, data flows, and control logic before syntax errors can distract you. The cost is minutes; the savings are hours.
